title: Habit close
hookLine: the habit stretch ends here: a practice is built, not willed into being

cards: New Year's resolutions have a reputation. Big promise on the first of January, grim jaw, white knuckles, and for some, a quiet surrender a few weeks in. The usual story says the people who failed didn't want it enough.
They lacked willpower. The habit days on this path have told a different story. Routines live in places, hang on cues, start tiny, survive a slip.
Nowhere in that list is gritted teeth. Today closes the habit stretch, and it comes down to three words.

teach.h: THE WALL: A FIGHT EVERY MORNING.
teach.b: Built, not willed. Start with the willpower picture. A habit is a wall you push against every day until you win or collapse.
Every morning is a fresh fight. It's exhausting, and it makes every lapse feel like a verdict on your character. Now the builder's picture.
A habit is a path across a field. The first walk is through tall grass. The tenth is easier.
By the hundredth there's a track, and your feet find it without being told. The work isn't pushing harder; it's walking the same way, in the same place, after the same cue, often enough.
William James, the American psychologist, wrote a long chapter on habit in his Principles of Psychology.
One line fits this whole stretch: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy."

Not a prisoner to be forced, not an enemy to be beaten: an ally that carries the load once the track is laid. The builder's picture changes what a bad day means. The willpower picture concludes, "I'm weak."
The builder asks something practical: was the cue missing?

teach.h: A BAD DAY IS A REPAIR JOB.
teach.b: Was the start too big? Did the place change? Those are things a person can fix by Thursday.
And a good day isn't a triumph of will. Just one more walk across the field.

how: People who keep a long practice often describe it as something they built gradually, by repeating it in the same place after the same cue, rather than something they forced through willpower; William James wrote of making the nervous system an ally.

o: a habit you keep only with daily willpower
the end of the habit days: a path worn by walking
the moment a habit finally can't be broken

games.q: two pictures of a habit: tap the pairs.
p: a wall you push against every day
make the nervous system our ally
a bad day, to a builder
a repair job, not a verdict

s: the habit days said willpower is the key to a lasting practice
they pointed to place, cue, a tiny start and a reason of your own.
William James wanted the nervous system to be an ally, not an enemy
that's his line from the habit chapter of The Principles of Psychology.

games.q: your practice slipped three days running. what does the builder ask?
o: was the cue missing, or the start too big?
games.why: the builder's picture turns a lapse into a practical question: which part of the design needs fixing.

practice: Bring out your four lines, or picture them, and read them once, slowly; then set them, or picture them, where the cue happens: by the kettle, on the car dashboard, beside the chair.
Lower the eyes and sit, and let this sit be one more walk across the field, nothing more.

wordCard.voice: Habit close. The end of the habit stretch: a practice grows the way a path does, by walking it, not by forcing it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: built, not willed. A slip is a repair job, not a verdict. That's the habit stretch, closed.
